10dz9l274b6: Ethereum's beacon chain signs using the elliptic curve BLS12-381, but BIP32, the previously widely used key derivation standard, does not fit this curve. BIP32 discards values larger than the curve's order as invalid keys, and given BLS12-381's private key subgroup order and the entropy size used, more than 54% of keys generated via BIP32 end up invalid. Furthermore, if a standard is introduced after users have already begun generating keys, tools diverge in their approaches, making it hard to move between key management systems. Finally, to prepare for a scenario where a sudden advance in quantum computing renders BLS12-381 insecure, a mechanism is needed to switch to a new signature scheme using pre-shared public keys. This standard solves all three problems at once.

The registry is a single contract that links every registered name to its responsible resolver and lets the name owner change the resolver address or create subnames. A subname can have a different owner from its parent name. The resolver handles the actual resource lookup for a name and returns a contract address, content hash, IP address and so on. The registrar allocates names to users and is the only entity that can update ENS. In the registry, the owner of a node is that node's registrar. A registrar can be a contract or an externally owned account, but the root and top-level registrars are expected to be implemented at least as contracts. Name resolution has two steps. First, the name is hashed and the resolver address is obtained from the registry, and then the function matching the resource type is called on the resolver. Because namehash is determined by the name alone, it can be computed in advance and put into a contract, and lookup is O(1) regardless of the number of components in the name.

For example, a derivative NFT references an original NFT. However, the existing royalty standard ERC-2981 does not consider such reference structures at all, and it does not support specifying multiple recipients at a single level. As a result, even for a work made jointly by a creator and collaborators, royalties could only be sent to a single address, and when a derivative was sold there was no way for rewards to flow to the referenced original. This standard allows multiple recipients per work, splits royalties along the reference graph down to a set depth, and lets the fixed rate be queried without a sale, giving marketplaces and users a transparent reward structure.

Benefits attached to an NFT, such as discount coupons, voting rights, or airdrop claim rights, are not recorded on chain. As a result, granting such benefits requires issuing a separate new token, which is not bound to the original NFT. For example, if an airline distributes benefit tokens to attract CryptoPunks holders into its club, and the original NFT is later transferred to someone else, the benefit remains with the previous holder and the new holder does not automatically receive it. Conversely, if an NFT holder has no intention of using a benefit and wants to pass it to someone else, there is no way to separate ownership from the benefit, so the entire NFT must be transferred. 13x4we261u7: Until now, on chain signature verification has only handled cases where the signer has an Ethereum address. A regular account (EOA) signs with a private key, and ERC-1271 defines how smart accounts, such as multisigs, verify signatures, but in both cases the signer's identity is an Ethereum address. However, as account abstraction has advanced, keys other than the secp256k1 that Ethereum natively supports have become widely used: the secp256r1 curve supported by many mobile devices, RSA keys issued by traditional institutions, and zero knowledge (ZK) schemes that sign with JWTs from email or large web services. These keys have no Ethereum address to represent them. One could deploy an ERC-1271 compatible contract for each key, but that is cumbersome and expensive. Giving a key a fixed on chain address also risks assets being mistakenly sent to that address, which conflicts with account abstraction's direction of separating the account address that holds assets from the key that controls the account. This standard solves the problem by having a small number of verifier contracts per key type, and having accounts identify signers as (verifier, key) pairs.

149crugxht: When a contract needs to reference multiple off-chain documents, such as contracts, receipts, or certificates, implementations typically bundle the documents' hashes into a single value. Without a common rule, however, each implementation differs in how it lists document entries, the sort order, versioning, and handling of replacements. As a result, two systems holding exactly the same documents can compute different bundle hashes and lose interoperability. Mixing the normalization step, which converts original files into standardized bytes, with the manifest step, which lists those results to produce a hash, also means the entire rule set shifts whenever format-specific handling changes. This standard separates the two steps and fixes how the manifest is built and recorded on-chain, so that anyone with the same set of documents arrives at the same hash.

A namespace root must belong neither to this default tree nor to a tree derived from another namespace. That way, multiple namespaces can be used together with the default layout, intentionally or not, without collisions. `keccak256(id) - 1` is a location that Solidity does not use, but once a namespace grows beyond one slot it extends to `keccak256(id) + n`, which can overlap with the region Solidity may use, so it is not used as the final location. The hash is therefore applied once more, so that the namespace is fully separated from the default storage under the assumptions of keccak256 collision resistance and no abnormally large arrays. The trailing `& ~0xff` aligns the location to a multiple of 256. This is an optimization anticipating that, after the transition to the Verkle state tree, the gas schedule will change and a group of 256 slots may become warm all at once.

1askt871hrq: The reason for standardizing storage slots instead of giving the proxy a public function that returns the logic address is function selector collisions. The ABI uses only a 4-byte selector to tell functions apart, so functions with different names can have the same selector. If a function on the proxy collides with a function on the logic contract, the call is not forwarded to the logic contract and the proxy intercepts it and returns its own value. Citing the Nomic Labs article Malicious backdoors in Ethereum proxies, the original text explains that the compiler catches collisions within one contract but not between contracts, so collisions can be abused to hide a backdoor in a contract that looks normal. 1bae6t9w3t: rootOwnerOf and rootOwnerOfChild walk back up the tree following ownership relationships. If a bottom-up token has a parent, rootOwnerOf is called on the parent; if that fails, rootOwnerOfChild is called; and if that also fails, the token's owner address is treated as the root. Since it cannot be known in advance whether the counterpart contract has the relevant function, the actual call must be made via staticcall in assembly to check for failure and prevent state changes. In the returned bytes32 value, the first 4 bytes hold the magic value 0xcd740db5, and the last 20 bytes hold the address. This value is the XOR of the four selectors rootOwnerOf, rootOwnerOfChild, tokenOwnerOf, and ownerOfChild. In calls where the existence of the function is uncertain, the first 4 bytes must always be compared against this value to confirm it is a valid return. Top-down and bottom-up are mutually compatible, so rootOwnerOf returns the topmost address regardless of the configuration.

Because of this structure, other modules cannot reuse an already well-built signature verification logic even if they want to, and similar verification code must be rewritten every time a new validator is created. Also, even if an account wants to use authorization logic directly to decide whether to allow a transaction based on what it is trying to do, there was no standardized module type for this, forcing reliance on external modules. This proposal defines new module types such as policies, signers, and stateless validators so that this logic can be divided and reused in a standardized way.

1fqcbi0ir4r: The ECDSA signatures widely used in Ethereum are typically conveyed as three values, v, r, and s, occupying 96 bytes under Solidity ABI encoding. However, a recoverable ECDSA signature has the property that flipping both s and v together still produces a valid signature. This means two valid signatures with different shapes can exist for the same message, a property called malleability. Also, v occupies only one degree of freedom in the signature, yet it must be encoded every time, which wastes space. This standard fixes v to a single value of 27 and removes v from the signature entirely. As a result, the signature becomes just 64 bytes consisting of r and s, and the variant signature with s and v flipped is no longer valid, which also eliminates the malleability problem.

1hwjjurrs1z: A regular account (EOA) transaction only needs its balance, nonce, and signature checked, and once a transaction is confirmed valid, it cannot become invalid without that account paying a fee. This makes mass-submission attacks economically infeasible, since costs spiral. Account abstraction, by contrast, performs validation using arbitrary EVM code that can depend on storage or block information. This makes it possible to craft a UserOperation that passes in the mempool but fails when included in a block, and a single storage change could invalidate huge numbers of unrelated UserOperations at once. An attacker can pay almost no fees while dumping free computation on bundlers, making it computationally infeasible to maintain a mempool containing only valid UserOperations. Also, if spam criteria differ from node to node, nodes may end up treating each other as spammers, splitting the network, so a shared validation rule across all nodes is needed.

In a proxy structure, where several functional modules share one storage, different modules can write to the same location and overwrite each other's data. However, this approach was not a formal standard for a long time. ERC-7201, published in 2023, standardized a pattern with the same purpose but proposed a different calculation formula from the Diamond Storage already in use. If the interface changes in a new version, existing integrations can break, and there is no standard way to migrate to the new version gradually. Trust is an even bigger problem. Even if an admin key or governance is compromised and malicious code is deployed, users have no choice but to use that latest implementation, and they cannot escape a harmful upgrade unless they stop using the contract entirely. In the end, users must trust the administrator or governance forever, with no way to choose and trust only a specific version that has been audited and verified. This standard solves this problem with a proxy interface that keeps previous versions open.

1kq2fgc6qzg: Smart contract languages such as Solidity and Vyper use a tree-shaped storage layout that places state variables in order starting from slot 0. This is sufficient for most contracts, but it causes problems in some design patterns. In modular designs that execute the code of several contracts with DELEGATECALL while sharing the same storage, each piece of code must carefully coordinate how it uses storage. In upgradeable contracts, adding a state variable during an upgrade can affect the storage locations of existing variables, which makes adding variables difficult. For this reason, a method of placing a group of variables at a pseudorandom location obtained by hashing is used, but values placed this way are not declared as Solidity state variables and are therefore invisible to the compiler. Tools such as static analyzers and block explorers need to know where a contract's data is, and if the way locations are determined is not standardized, they cannot interpret such contracts correctly.

1lj5q2obczo: Many projects raise funds by issuing tokens, but an ordinary ERC-20 token is not directly tied to the revenue the project earns. Since holders receive no share, there is little reason to hold the token long term, and there is no minimal mechanism backing the token's value. In particular, open source projects and open source AI models have no good way to turn contributions into money, which weakens the motivation of both contributors and organizations. This standard pools revenue arriving from multiple sources into a single common revenue pool, making the token itself represent a share of that pool. Holders can claim a portion of the revenue at each cycle, and if they wish, they can burn the token to immediately withdraw their share from the pool. Thanks to this burn mechanism, as long as there is money in the pool, the token's value is guaranteed to be at least equal to its share of the pool.

Examples include whether a given credential is still valid, or which issuers can be trusted. In practice, however, verifiable claims alone are not enough; supporting information is also needed to confirm whether a claim has been revoked or whether its issuer is trustworthy. Without a standard for managing this information structurally on-chain, each ecosystem ends up building its own ad hoc approach, making it hard for participants to establish and maintain trust with one another. This standard calls this supporting information a hint and defines a common contract interface that lets anyone create and manage a hint list under their own address. 1mxfmwicf3a: Zero-knowledge proofs (zk-SNARKs) let you prove you belong to a certain set without revealing your identity. But applications like voting or airdrops, where each person should participate only once, need a way to stop the same account from participating twice. Ethereum's ECDSA signatures can produce different results for the same message, and anyone wanting to verify deterministic generation would need the secret key itself. Copying the secret key into a proving program is risky, and hardware wallets sometimes never expose the secret key at all. Running an entire proof system inside a secure chip is also impractical. So a new signature scheme is needed that produces one unique value per account without ever exporting the secret key, while letting anyone verify that the value was constructed correctly using only the public key.

It must revert if there is already an accepted delegation, the expiration time must be in the future, and it reverts if the delegate is the owner themselves or the zero address. Any prior pending proposal is replaced. It only takes effect once the delegate (or their operator) calls acceptOwnershipDelegation, after which the delegate is recorded as the ownership manager until expiration. stopOwnershipDelegation can only be called by the delegate side for an accepted delegation, and on success the owner becomes the ownership manager again. Unlike approve or setApprovalForAll, which only add permissions while the owner keeps their status, delegation transfers the owner's rights themselves to the delegate and reverts automatically on expiration. 1nti7qwtwvp: When a CCIP Read-aware contract calls another contract that may also implement CCIP Read, it must catch every OffchainLookup thrown by the other contract and revert with a different error if sender differs from the other contract's address. It may also replace every OffchainLookup with a different error, which avoids implementing nested support but makes nested lookups impossible. The default nested-call error propagation in Solidity must not be left as is. If A calls B, which does not know CCIP, and B calls A back so that A throws OffchainLookup, then B and A propagate it in turn, and an error whose sender matches A and looks valid reaches the client, but in reality only the inner call completes. The NestedLookup example in the source shows how to catch the other contract's error, check sender, and then rethrow it bundled with its own aCallback selector, the other contract's address, the other contract's callback, and the other contract's extraData.

1o0r9r4c3zf: An NFT is originally meant to represent only a single unique asset, such as an artwork or game item, and there was no standard way to hold other tokens inside it. As a result, services that need to handle a unique asset bundled together with a fungible token, such as games, had to invent project-specific methods. Additionally, ERC-20 tokens have no standard way to notify the recipient of an incoming transfer, so simply sending tokens to an NFT contract address leaves no way to know which NFT they were intended for. Furthermore, there was no common mechanism to prevent a seller of a token-holding NFT from secretly withdrawing the tokens inside it right before a sale closes. This standard aims to solve these problems by defining common functions for depositing and withdrawing ERC-20 tokens from a specific NFT, along with a counter (nonce) that increments with every withdrawal.

1p0ft1y0w51: On a blockchain, anyone can see the contents of a transaction before it is processed. Actions that need secrecy, such as voting, therefore expose their contents and suffer harms such as front-running, where someone sees another party's transaction and jumps ahead of it, back-running, where someone follows right behind it, and sandwich attacks, which wrap a transaction on both sides. The long-standing remedy is commit-reveal. You first submit only the hash of the content to lock in a commitment, then reveal the original later to have it verified. However, if each standard, such as voting standards and token standards, designs its own commit scheme, they are incompatible with one another. This standard fixes a single commit function as the common piece and leaves the reveal method to each application, so commit-reveal can be added anywhere without changing the function signatures of existing standards.

1p5svk87vc5: EIP-712 is a way of signing structured messages. To prevent replay attacks, where a signature is reused elsewhere, and to reduce phishing, it uses a domain separator that binds a signature to a domain such as a specific contract. The domain consists of a name, version, chain ID, verifying contract address, and optional fields such as a salt, but EIP-712 itself does not define how a contract can announce which fields it uses and with what values. As a result, apps had to fit the domain separately for each contract, and generic integration was impossible. The original text points out that even EIP-2612 (permit), known to greatly improve user experience, has not been widely adopted for this reason. The DOMAIN_SEPARATOR function of EIP-2612 returns only a hash value, so it cannot be used to show the user the domain contents and verify them before signing. This standard fills the gap by defining an interface through which an app can read a contract's domain definition.

1pb24432oiv: The two concepts were separated because they represent fundamentally different relationships. Jurisdiction is voluntary: a contract can unilaterally declare that it will follow a given system's rules. Accreditation, by contrast, requires external approval: only the authority can formally recognize a contract as an accepted participant in its system. Jurisdiction expresses alignment, while accreditation expresses acceptance, and declaring a jurisdiction does not mean the authority has recognized that contract. Also, because an authority typically only imposes enforcement on contracts it has accredited, it is accreditation that creates the enforcement pathway. This distinction reflects how real-world institutions actually work: following a system's rules is a self-declaration, but gaining formal status within it requires explicit action by the authority.

1qoaj0t4jfn: Built on top of the Chaum-Pedersen signature scheme. Given a 32-byte message m and a keypair (sk, pk), a random r is drawn, h = htc([m, sec1(pk)]) is computed, and then z = h^r, the nullifier nul = h^sk, c = sha256([g, pk, h, nul, g^r, z]), and s = r + sk*c are computed. The signature is (z, s, g^r, c, nul). The key idea is computing h from the hash of the message and pk rather than the message and r, which is what makes the nullifier deterministic. The signature contains both a deterministic part (the nullifier) and a non-deterministic part.

1r0wab74x1h: On Ethereum, signatures made by an externally owned account (EOA) can be verified with ecrecover(), and signatures made by a smart contract can be verified with ERC-1271, but there was no standard way to verify a signature made by an NFT. For example, suppose a DAO represents roles such as CEO and COO as NFT badges and replaces the holders by election every quarter. An agreement or approval signed by the sitting COO is then tied to that person's personal account at the time, not to the 'COO role'. When the person changes, past signatures do not move along with the role. Workarounds exist, such as using the DAO's multisig wallet or installing a contract as COO, but they make it hard to divide responsibility finely or add unnecessary complexity. This standard solves the problem by tying signatures to a transferable NFT.

1r1clvgnky8: A transfer by NFT ID is simple: the NFT and its entire attached fractional value (10 ** decimals()) move together. A fractional-quantity transfer, on the other hand, requires managing NFT allocation and falls into three cases. First, if neither side's whole-unit balance changes, NFT allocation stays the same. Second, if the sender's balance drops below a whole unit, a proportional number of NFTs must be removed from their holdings. Third, if the recipient's balance crosses a whole unit, their NFT holdings must be increased proportionally. The standard does not mandate a specific handling method, but common examples given are minting/burning tokens in a monotonically increasing fashion or tracking NFT ownership with a stack or queue.

1smi4fq3nk5: NFTs often suffer from poor market liquidity because prices are not transparent. Once you buy one, it is hard to know how much you could resell it for, and if you cannot find a buyer, you cannot cash out at all. This standard solves the problem by introducing the role of guarantor. When multiple groups of guarantors each offer different price guarantees for the same NFT, that itself becomes a multi-sided price evaluation system for the NFT. A buyer can at any time return the NFT to a guarantor at the highest guaranteed price and recover funds to limit losses. A guarantor who fulfills a guarantee obligation can in turn demand fulfillment from the next guarantor in the sequence. Because a guarantor can be a DAO, the NFT can continue to be operated as a DAO after ownership passes to the guarantor, building social or community recognition.

The public inputs are the instruction's Merkle root root, the debtor and creditor data hashes debtorHash and creditorHash, the amount range minAmountMilli and maxAmountMilli, the currency hash currencyHash, and the expiry. Both key generation and verification are batch operations: there must be exactly one result per requested keyId, and duplicate, missing, unrequested, or partial-batch entries must be rejected. The verification result is authoritative as a single `verified` value; per-key partial success is not represented. Two fulfillment modes are permitted. 1tt630r6hsk: The existing NFT standard (ERC-721) uses a sole-ownership model in which a token has exactly one owner. Digital assets such as files, however, do not lose quality when copied and can be held by many people, and the sole-ownership model cannot capture this. Passing ownership strips the original owner of their rights, so a structure in which several people jointly own the same asset cannot be built in a standard way. The standard also has no mechanism for the party who first provided an asset to keep earning rewards as it circulates afterward. This standard supports joint ownership by adding the new owner to a list on transfer instead of removing the existing owner, and it sends a set fee to the provider on every transfer so that creators and providers are rewarded. It also defines an archive mechanism through which an owner voluntarily gives up the right to transfer.

Also, if membership is split only into member and non-member, it is hard to naturally express tiered benefits that vary with holdings or voting power proportional to holdings. On success, the record is preserved but permanently marked invalid. It is excluded from the latest value, the provider's latest value, the current chain, quorum, aggregation, and deviation calculations, and affected pointers are recalculated. If an original is invalidated, that provider and timestamp slot can be refilled with a new original, and if a correction is invalidated, the preceding snapshot becomes terminal again and a replacement correction can be submitted. 1u31fsxekl9: Implementations must use the constant NO_CORRECTION = type(uint256).max, and when correctsIndex equals this value the snapshot is an original. If correctedByIndex is 0, the snapshot is a terminal snapshot not yet corrected, since a correction's index is always greater than its target's, making 0 a safe sentinel. A correction must reference a prior snapshot with the same subjectId, and must use the same indicatorId, periodStart, and periodEnd as the target, and may only correct a snapshot whose correctedByIndex is 0. When a correction is accepted, only the target's correctedByIndex changes to the new index; all other fields remain unchanged. Each snapshot can be corrected at most once, which keeps the chain linear and prevents branching. Reporting authority alone must not be allowed to permit correcting another reporter's record; authority may instead be granted to the original reporter, a designated corrector, or an administrator.

1ujj3j0uv43: A relayer (bundler) that submits transactions on behalf of a smart contract wallet has difficulty knowing in advance whether that transaction will actually pay its fee. Verifying this requires actually executing the entire transaction, and if a malicious user changes state right before execution to make the transaction fail, the bundler wastes gas for nothing. Also, since even a small change in chain state can invalidate transactions without any way to know which ones, the entire mempool must be continually re-checked. Conversely, trying to solve this by strictly standardizing the transaction format would require every already-deployed smart contract wallet to be individually upgraded, and would reduce the freedom to design new wallets. This standard tries to solve both problems at once by delegating the determination responsibility to an endorser contract built by the wallet developer.

Because the interpretation is not part of on-chain execution, complex decoding and validation can be done without gas-cost constraints. The resolver is the point of trust: solver operators whitelist resolver addresses they have verified through audits, bounties, and similar means, and they trust the instructions those resolvers produce. A resolver must guarantee that an order can only be aborted in the cases specified by its RevertPolicy, and that unless the abort policy is triggered, the solver that began execution will be able to fulfill all requirements and receive all payments.

1wfmktz43n8: The Ethereum ecosystem is heading toward hundreds, and eventually thousands, of layer 2 (L2) chains that use the same address format as mainnet. An address alone does not reveal which chain it belongs to, creating the risk of sending funds to an unreachable address on the wrong chain. The earlier standard ERC-7930 defined a binary format for holding an address on a specific chain, but it is suited to low-level uses such as contracts and carries no meaning for humans. In addition, the mapping between chain names and identifiers has been managed since EIP-155 through centralized off-chain lists, which cannot keep up with the growing number of chains, depend on a trusted central administrator, and cannot support non-Ethereum-family chains. This standard solves the problem by defining a human-readable chain-qualified address format together with an on-chain registry that lets chain operators register their own chain information directly.

1wlatpoawy: An interoperable address is a binary value consisting of the fields Version, ChainType, ChainReferenceLength, ChainReference, AddressLength, and Address in that order. Version is 2 bytes and must be 0x0001 in big-endian for this specification (version 1). ChainType is a 2-byte value corresponding to a CASA namespace, and it determines how the following ChainReference and Address are interpreted and displayed. ChainReferenceLength is a 1-byte integer holding the byte length of ChainReference, and ChainReference is a variable-length binary value pointing to the chain. AddressLength is a 1-byte integer holding the byte length of Address, and Address is the variable-length binary encoding of the serialized address. Because length fields precede the data, arbitrary-length data can be held.

1wy8ivgia63: Storing the script directly in the contract has three drawbacks. First, every update requires the contract's signing key, so the key is exposed more often. Second, updating requires a contract call, which becomes a cost barrier if updates are frequent. Third, client scripts are usually much larger than contracts, so storage fees are high. So frequently changing functionality is placed in an external resource, and the contract only tells where it is. The external resource can be centralized hosting such as the cloud, a personal server, or decentralized storage such as IPFS. Fully decentralized storage can be disadvantageous in speed, price, and capacity, so this standard returns multiple URIs as an array, allowing centralized, personal, and decentralized locations to be mixed. The script itself can point to other scripts or data sources to enable extensions such as lazy loading, and the integrity handling of such secondary data is left to the script format.

1x2pslnx1ui: Bundling is the process in which a bundler collects multiple UserOperations and makes them into one transaction. A UserOperation that accesses the sender address of another UserOperation in the same bundle, or whose validation accesses an address created by a factory for another UserOperation, must be excluded, and for each paymaster the bundler must track whether the deposit covers all of its UserOperations. After building the bundle, it runs debug_traceCall with the maximum gas to verify the opcode and storage access rules and the whole handleOps transaction, and uses the gas consumed for the actual transaction. If it reverts, the entity that the EntryPoint called last with CALL in the trace is taken as the cause (it does not assume FailedOp), and the corresponding UserOperation is removed from the bundle and the mempool. If the cause is a factory or paymaster and the sender is not staked, that factory or paymaster is blocked, and if the sender is staked, the sender is blocked instead. This is repeated until debug_traceCall succeeds. This presupposes a reputation system that throttles or temporarily bans global entities (paymasters and factories) that invalidate multiple UserOperations, and stake is required to prevent Sybil attacks. Stake is not enforced on-chain; each bundler checks it during simulation, and staked entities get relaxed storage usage limits. Because UserOperations from unrelated senders can enter the same transaction, contracts that use EIP-1153 transient storage must clean up on their own any transient storage used for sensitive information or access control.

1zvchn3vqjb: The supplier appends a nonce derived from block height h (typically the block hash) to the end of each chunk, finds the leaf m that produces the smallest new Merkle root, and submits the extracted path m_path and leaf value m_leaf_data. The on-chain verification function verifyDataProof rejects the proof as expired if the difference between the current block and h exceeds MAX_BLOCK_DISTANCE, and checks whether the lower 192 bits of the root reconstructed from the path match the MixHash. It then computes proof_result with the nonce appended, and if the result is smaller than the existing one, it emits a ProofPunish event flagging the previous submitter for a penalty and updates the result. The network cannot directly verify the optimality of a proof and instead relies on challenges from other suppliers who know of a better proof. As a result, some EIP-721 and EIP-1155 implementations have handled minting and burning by borrowing the transfer function or similar methods. However, minting and burning change a token's total supply, and the access control rules that decide who can do them usually differ from those for transfers. Mixing minting and burning into the transfer function makes implementations more complex and makes mistakes in permission settings more likely. This standard aims to simplify implementations and reduce security errors by defining dedicated mint and burn functions suited to each of the three token standards.

249aw5c5yei: Segments within a single intent always execute in the order given in the segments array. The order between intents is specified by the order array. For example, if order is [1,1,0,1], segments 1 and 2 of the second intent execute first, then segment 1 of the first intent, then segment 3 of the second intent. If no order is specified, or if order is exhausted while segments remain, the default order is used, cycling from the first intent to the last. If an intent that has already finished all its segments is referenced again, that call is skipped. The bytes returned by executeIntentSegment are remembered by the entry point and passed back as context on the next call for the same intent. This lets a standard track state changes even while other intents execute in between, such as a standard that sends out one token and then checks whether a different token was received.

24bbvhclqzl: To send an ERC-20 token, the sender must submit the transaction themselves and pay the fee (gas) in ether (ETH). This creates a problem for users who hold tokens but no ether: they cannot transfer at all. ERC-2612, which serves the same purpose, uses a sequential number (nonce), so creating several transactions at once can cause number collisions, or a miner reordering transactions can cause failures. These failures become more frequent when gas fees are high and transactions sit in the queue for a long time. In addition, ERC-20's approve/transferFrom pattern is vulnerable to multiple-withdrawal attacks and encourages bad habits like unlimited approvals. ERC-777 and other proposals meant to replace it failed to gain wide adoption due to compatibility and security issues. A way was therefore needed to safely delegate transfers with a single signature, without relying on the approval pattern.

The initiator can watch exchange rate movements during that window and only complete the trade when it favors them, simply abandoning it otherwise. This is effectively the same as a financial American call option, yet the initiator pays no premium for that option, leaving the counterparty unilaterally disadvantaged. However, handling voting purely through the balance query (balanceOf) that most tokens provide creates two problems. First, because balances are not recorded per point in time, a person could vote and then move their tokens to another account to vote again with the same tokens. Second, there is no way to hand off only voting power to someone else without transferring ownership of the tokens outright. As a result, with existing asset-linked ERC-721 tokens, there is no guarantee that legal ownership of the underlying real-world asset transfers along with the token when it is sent to someone else. In the United States, ownership changes are sometimes recorded on paper at the county recorder's office, making it practically impossible to update this manual record every time an NFT trades. This standard attempts to bridge this gap by attaching immutable information identifying the specific property and a hash of the legal rights documents to the token, presenting a common structure that lets rights to the property transfer atomically, that is, together in one step, with the NFT transfer.

The ComplianceAuthorization struct consists of the fields token, authority, operationHash, policyId, contextHash, nonce, validAfter, and validBefore, where token must equal address(this) and the validity period is from validAfter (inclusive) to validBefore (exclusive). operationHash is computed by binding the caller, the parties, the id, the amount, and application data, so it cannot be reused for a different transfer. 27diyxfftds: A blob introduced by EIP-4844 is 128KiB (4,096 field elements), but many rollups cannot fill this space. According to a 26-rollup analysis cited in the source, large rollups fill it nearly completely while small rollups often use less than 5%, and sharing could save 80-99% on data availability costs. However, even when multiple parties want to split a single blob, there has been no standard for announcing who uses which range, so each project has built its own events, dedicated registries, and separate indexing methods, leading to fragmentation where tools are incompatible with each other. Whoever posts the blob is already paying the full data availability cost for all 128KiB, so the remaining field elements go to waste. A standard declaration interface would let the unused space be opened to other protocols at no additional data cost.

ERC-2612 for ERC-20 tokens and ERC-4494 for ERC-721 NFTs can each authorize only one action (transfer or safeTransferFrom), allow only a single approver, and typically require two steps: sending a permit transaction first and then a transfer transaction. As a result, authorizing arbitrary functions by signature, aggregating approvals from multiple people to function like multisig or threshold signatures, or building flows where someone else submits the transaction on your behalf each required a separate design per function. Otherwise a logic contract could overwrite proxy information while writing to its own variables. Solidity linearizes the inheritance chain and then places the first variable in the first slot and the next in the following slot, in order of declaration. Only the values of dynamic arrays and mappings are stored at a hash location formed by concatenating the key and the slot number. The Solidity team confirmed that this storage layout is part of the language's external interface, so changing it would be treated as a breaking change. Vyper follows the same approach. The standard slots are hashes of strings that do not start with a storage index, so they do not overlap with slots the compiler assigns. However, existing token standards do not standardize these features, so each issuer must implement them differently, making it hard for wallets or trading services to integrate in a common way. 2aa6dn9lxvf: The existing ERC-721 has only a single role, Owner. So to stake, pledge as collateral, or lend an NFT, the token itself has to be transferred to and locked in that contract. But many apps grant benefits like airdrops or tier-based rewards using the fact that a token sits in a wallet as proof of holding. Once a token is locked in a contract, the original owner loses access to those benefits, and reward systems can only fix this by individually supporting as many locking contracts as possible. There has also been no standard way to express use cases like lending or delegation, where the owner stays the same but the user changes, which has always made it hard to build such services on top of ERC-721. This standard tries to solve the problem by dividing use cases into contexts handled by controllers, and by adding ownership delegation to the standard, which separates the owner from the right to exercise ownership.

2aarkfxonej: ERC-8001 defines only the minimal functionality for multi-agent coordination, leaving reputation and trust decisions to be handled as modules. As a result, an agent looking to initiate coordination has no common way to answer questions like "should this agent be allowed into the coordination" or "can this agent's judgment in vouching for other agents be trusted." A central registry would solve the problem of establishing trust with an unfamiliar agent, but it would mean relying on a single operating entity. Using addresses directly as identifiers also has the problem that accumulated trust records break whenever a key is rotated. This standard borrows the web-of-trust model from OpenPGP, proven over more than 25 years, recording trust against ENS names, which survive key rotation, as identifiers and propagating it along paths.

As a result, even when an external tool pre-executes a transaction such as a token transfer (an off-chain simulation), it cannot be certain exactly where the ownership data is actually recorded. Simulation then ends up relying heavily on the events the contract emits, but the original text points out that events are only reference information and the sole source of truth should be state (storage). Protocol dispatch (EXECUTION_ROUTE_PROTOCOL, 0x00) has SENDER frames call the target directly with caller=tx.sender, without the account's code intervening, so all policy must be enforced at verification time. Contract dispatch (EXECUTION_ROUTE_CONTRACT, 0x01) has every SENDER frame target the account itself, calling ERC-7579's execute or executeFromExecutor with caller=tx.sender, so ERC-7579 execution modes, supportsExecutionMode, and hooks apply as usual. 2ce5buwiyaq: The proxy's core operation consists of four stages. Stage 1 copies the call data with CALLDATACOPY, building the arguments [0, 0, cds] (cds being the call data size) from two PUSH0s and CALLDATASIZE. Stage 2 is DELEGATECALL, which stacks the arguments [gas, address, 0, cds, 0, 0] and executes it, receiving the success flag suc. Stage 3 copies the return data with RETURNDATACOPY. Stage 4 branches on suc; since opcodes have no if/else, JUMPI and JUMPDEST are used. The JUMPI target is 0x2a; on success it passes through JUMPDEST to RETURN, and on failure it executes REVERT. The arguments for REVERT and RETURN, [0, rds], are prepared only once before the JUMPI to avoid duplication.

This function can reject the transfer by throwing, and if it returns anything other than the magic value, the transaction must be reverted. The message sender is always the NFT contract address. 2d05aznbgxe: A relay that signs two different transactions with the same nonce has its misbehavior proven on chain. The victim submits both transactions and signatures to penalizeRepeatedNonce, and the hub forfeits the relay's stake, giving half to the submitter and sending the other half to address(0) to be burned. The burn mechanism exists to prevent a dishonest relay from penalizing itself and getting away without a net loss. An attack where a relay signs with a nonce higher than the current one to delay execution is prevented by having the sender include a max_nonce value in the request (recommended to be 2 to 3 higher than the current nonce) and rejecting any transaction outside that range. In version 2, a Penalizer contract takes over this proof logic, and to prevent the reward from being intercepted, it requires a two-step process: first committing the hash of the penalty call, then making the actual call within an expiration deadline after a block delay.

The EntryPoint then calculates the maximum fee the sender will pay and the amount to add to the deposit, using the verification and execution gas limits and the current gas values, and calls the sender's validateUserOp. If any validateUserOp fails, at minimum that UserOperation's execution must be skipped, and the whole bundle may be reverted. Next, it checks that the account deposit covers the maximum cost. In the execution loop, the account is called with callData. If callData starts with the method signature of IAccountExecute.executeUserOp, it is encoded as executeUserOp(userOp,userOpHash) and called. After the call, the remainder of the prepaid cost is refunded to the deposit. However, if the unused gas in callGasLimit and paymasterPostOpGasLimit is 40000 (PENALTY_GAS_THRESHOLD) or more, a 10% penalty (UNUSED_GAS_PENALTY_PERCENT) is charged on that unused amount. This mechanism prevents a UserOperation from reserving gas space in a bundle without using it and thereby blocking other UserOperations. 2dyhfx81bw6: Because storing data on the blockchain is expensive, it is advantageous to compress resources such as website files before storing and serving them. On the regular web (HTTP), the client sends a list of compression methods it can decode (Accept-Encoding), and the server negotiates by compressing the response with one of them. 2fisjrp7s98: Without a view tag, the recipient must perform 2 elliptic curve multiplications (ecMUL), 2 hashes, and 1 elliptic curve addition (ecADD) for every announcement they check. With a view tag, most announcements are filtered out by hashing the shared secret and comparing only the first byte, so only 1 ecMUL and 1 hash are needed, and parsing time drops by about 6 times. Because the view tag is 1 byte, the probability of skipping the remaining computation for an announcement that is not yours is 255/256. In exchange, 1 byte of the shared secret is revealed, so the security margin falls from 128 bits to 124 bits. This reduction affects only privacy and does not affect the security of stealth address generation itself. The authors describe this as a tradeoff in which view tags improve off-chain efficiency at the cost of making the announcement event more complex.

2fp4gxrvfnk: On Ethereum, calling a contract requires paying gas fees in ETH. This means someone without ETH cannot use a dapp even if they have a wallet address, and it is hard for the dapp to grow its user base. Even if a dapp wants to cover gas fees on the user's behalf, or let the user pay through some other means such as fiat currency, there was no common way to do this. There are also users in restricted environments who cannot easily connect to the blockchain directly. This standard solves the problem without any protocol changes. A relay (a relaying node) receives the user's signed request over a public channel such as the web, pays the gas and submits it on the user's behalf, and a single hub contract trusted by everyone pays the relay's cost and fee out of the dapp's deposit. This gives relays a profit incentive, means censorship does not occur as long as even one honest relay exists, and lets misbehavior be proven and penalized on chain.
2fpghzhc2q8: Existing proposals for making NFTs lockable require an event announcing the lock state to be emitted every time a token is minted. This standard saves gas by announcing the default lock state that applies to all tokens with a single event at contract deployment, and afterwards emitting events only when an individual token's state actually changes. It also defines functions for querying the lock state, so that other contracts and marketplaces can easily check a token's current state.

2ftrkci9qbj: On Ethereum, transfers and approvals of NFTs (unique digital assets recorded on the blockchain) execute instantly with a single signature from the owner. If a wallet's private key leaks or a user signs a malicious request via phishing, there is no way to reverse the NFT transfer. The very structure that gives the blockchain its strength, placing full responsibility for data on the user, also becomes its weakness. There have been many real cases of NFT theft, and the conventional way to prevent theft, moving NFTs into a cold wallet (a storage wallet not connected to the internet), makes NFTs inconvenient to use. By placing a validation step before every transfer and approval, a thief would need to obtain both the user's address and the validator address at the same time, making for a much stronger anti-theft system.

The sequence is validated in the EntryPoint for each key, and if validation fails the UserOperation is invalid and the bundle is reverted. The sequence increases monotonically and sequentially per sender, and a new key can be introduced at any time with an arbitrary value, with its sequence starting at 0. The problem grows as smart accounts (ERC-4337) become more widespread. ERC-672, which came later, relied on reverse ENS, but the original text names two problems with it: it is needlessly complex, and ENS itself is a centralized contract managed by a multisig wallet. This works for individual conditions like holder status or balance, but there is no shared interface that multiple tokens can query for transferability between logical domains, such as jurisdictions, regulated venues, corporate networks, game economies, or DAO treasury boundaries. Such compatibility is directional, so a transfer allowed from A to B may not be allowed from B to A, and the same path may differ by asset class. Without a standard interface, each token or transfer controller must embed its own path table or attach to a proprietary registry, duplicating policy state and forcing integrators to learn a different lookup method for each implementation. This standard standardizes the narrow question of whether a transfer of a given asset class from a given source domain to a given destination domain is currently permitted. It does not answer whether a transfer will ultimately succeed; checks such as balance, holder eligibility, freezes, and sanctions remain separate.

5xh8r6hk7l: Tokenizing real-world assets such as securities or real estate brings regulation with it. Transfers may need to be allowed only to permitted users, and assets may need to be frozen and forcibly moved for law enforcement. Existing token standards such as ERC-20, ERC-721, and ERC-1155 have no structure to carry these requirements. As a result, each issuer attached compliance features in its own way, and a decentralized finance (DeFi) protocol that wanted to integrate with RWA tokens had to learn each token's different approach individually. Earlier attempts at a universal RWA standard enforced fine-grained role-based access control, mandatory on-chain allowlists, specific on-chain identity systems, and metadata handling, which imposed unnecessary complexity and gas costs even on simple use cases that need none of those features. The assets are also so varied that a single comprehensive framework that specifies everything is hard to build. What was needed was a minimal common interface that leaves implementation to each party and unifies only the outward appearance.

62cihwdo75: Two mechanisms prevent sourcing attacks, in which data is not stored locally but instead fetched over the network at the moment a proof is generated. First, a time limit. In an Ethereum-like network with a block time of about 15 seconds, setting MAX_BLOCK_DISTANCE = 2 means a proof must be generated and submitted within 30 seconds, which most external sources cannot complete a transfer within. Second, an economic game. Under a model that rewards the supplier who first submits a correct proof, the delay from an external source lowers the probability of success, making it less profitable than local storage. The defense success rate is defined as R = (TNetwork - TLocal) / AvgProofTime, and the success rate decreases as AvgProofTime grows.

ERC-20's approve only permits another account to move a certain amount, so if the owner sends the tokens elsewhere in the meantime, the promise is broken. To guarantee availability, the contract must physically hold the tokens, but doing so transfers ownership to the contract, so owner benefits like airdrops no longer reach the real owner. Also, when tokens are pooled in a single contract, a single transfer can drain them all, increasing the potential damage. The source introduces the widely used middleware pattern from industry, a general, repeatable pattern of wrapping a call with another call under the same call signature. This lets specialized security providers develop and maintain specific checks independently (independent security providers), combine layers to build a per-contract security profile (composability), update layers without changing the protected contract (upgradeability), and perform a wide range of checks such as access control, input sanitization, and output validation (flexibility). As a result, permission management features such as approve, which lets another address move your NFT on your behalf, and setApprovalForAll, are borne by the NFT contract itself. Under this structure, the NFT contract becomes more complex, and the risks that arise from the contract implementing approval functionality come along with it. At initialization, generators g1 and g2 are created, and a commitment C is generated from the data content, which is posted as the data's unique identifier when metadata is uploaded. When a verifier generates a random value z, the prover generates a proof P=(y, π) and verification is done via e(π, yg1-zg2) = e(C - y*g1, g2). 928zl83ojz: Ethereum tokens have so far been split into two camps. ERC-20 is a fungible token in which every unit is identical, and ERC-721 is a non-fungible token (NFT) in which each token is distinct. However, ERC-20 requires a separate new contract for each asset with a different data structure or combination of attributes, so in practice a huge number of ERC-20 contracts get created. Conversely, ERC-721 has no concept of quantity, which is a major disadvantage for calculation, liquidity and management. For example, if financial products such as bonds, insurance policies or vesting plans are built as ERC-721, there is no standard interface for handling the value inside the token, so it is impossible to transfer just part of the stake the token represents. This calls for a semi-fungible token that combines the quantity feature of ERC-20 with the individual attributes of ERC-721. Making it backward compatible with ERC-721 lets it reuse infrastructure that is already in use, which also speeds up adoption.

With an ordinary externally owned account (EOA) wallet, the user must confirm each operation separately, and if approve succeeds but transferFrom fails, the approval remains in place and creates a security risk. To be safe, atomicity is needed so that if one operation fails, the entire bundle of operations fails. In addition, the struct array format commonly used to bundle multiple calls encodes each item's type information along with it, which makes the data larger and increases gas costs. A file must be split into 1KB chunks, with the final chunk zero-padded. e3phu5z0du: The original text explains why each element was removed from ERC-1155. First, mandatory callbacks are a burden for implementers who do not need callbacks or want to use their own mechanism, so they were removed. This reduces contract size, gas, and complexity. Second, batch processing is useful, but it is better decided per implementation than fixed in the standard. In environments such as rollups, where calldata is written to global storage, the calldata layout may need to be arranged differently. Third, the names safeTransfer and safeTransferFrom are misleading, because in practice they make an external call to a recipient account that has code and hand execution flow to an arbitrary contract. Removing both the mandatory callbacks and the word safe makes the default control flow safer. Fourth, because some methods are missing, it is not backward compatible with ERC-1155, but wrappers for ERC-20, ERC-721, and ERC-1155 can be built.

Once such a permission structure is set, it is hard to change to meet new requirements, and it is also difficult to dynamically grant only a limited set of permissions. eao1mj1nsr: Ethereum uses several token standards side by side, but they are not compatible with each other. Because the most widely used ERC-20 already has an established ecosystem, even when a new standard appears there is no defined procedure for migrating to it, creating a bottleneck that blocks adoption. Token developers must pick one standard at deployment time and stick with it, with no way to use the advantages of another standard even if they want to. On top of that, implementations of the same ERC-20 vary significantly. The source points out that, regarding the return value of the transfer function, tokens are inconsistent: some return true on success and revert on failure, some return false, and some have no return value at all (most notably USDT), making them incompatible with each other. This proposal aims to provide a shared conversion service that lets anyone create a different-standard version of an existing token, so that two versions can coexist and be exchanged for each other without needing to choose only one standard.

Attackers exploit this weakness by mass-generating (mining) addresses that resemble the victim's counterparty at the start and end, then injecting fake ERC-20 Transfer events into the transaction history. According to the original text, such address spoofing attacks have caused tens of thousands of ether and countless tokens to be sent to the wrong place, with fake events wasting network resources and complicating blockchain accounting. hcbxldvwi: On Ethereum, approving anything requires signing with a private key. A private key is a long, random value that cannot be memorized, and there is no way to change it once it has leaked. This is a significant barrier to entry, especially for users with little technical experience. Custodial services that hold private keys on a user's behalf are convenient but create dependence on a specific provider and run counter to decentralization. This standard uses the familiar concept of a password as a signing method. The user only needs to generate a zero-knowledge proof that they know the password and submit it; a smart contract verifies that proof on-chain. The password itself is never stored or transmitted anywhere and can be changed whenever needed. Rather than replacing the private key, it is an additional signing method layered on top of it, so even if the private key leaks, the password provides an extra layer of protection.

If the victim copies an address from their transaction history and sends funds, the assets go straight to the attacker. When a user publishes an o-transaction with nonce k+1 on one chain, the account nonce on other chains is still k, so an off-chain synchronizer detects this discrepancy and relays the data. Synchronizers race to relay it because of the reward, and the reward strategy (fees, mining-style rewards, etc.) is determined by the token deployer. i37fgk84ds: Today, identity verification is mostly handled by central authorities. The process is cumbersome, personal data gathered in one place is easily exposed to breaches, and users cannot control their own identity data. Blockchain-based decentralized identity (DID) solutions have emerged as an alternative, but existing approaches handle many attributes and interactions, so their structure is complex and developers and users find them hard to adopt. This standard does the opposite and keeps the structure as simple as possible. On-chain, it records only the address, the hash, and the verification status, and leaves detailed identity attributes such as name or age, along with the actual verification procedure, to off-chain systems. As a result, sensitive information is not stored directly on the blockchain, so privacy is protected, and because it is easy to integrate into dapps, it can aim for broader adoption.

i6ce6guql1: A transaction hash is a unique value that identifies a single transaction recorded on a blockchain, but the hash alone does not reveal which chain the transaction occurred on. The Ethereum ecosystem has many chains distinguished by number (chain ID), so looking up a transaction by hash always requires finding out separately which chain it is on. The transaction object inside a chain contains the chain ID, but it carries too much unnecessary data to be used for locating a transaction. This standard puts the chain ID and the hash into one string, so that the correct chain can be found easily from that one string alone. For example, it can be used in a forwarder service that takes such a string and routes it to the appropriate blockchain explorer.

iun6chbsd5: Approval mode is a uint8 bitmask where only two bits carry meaning. Bit 0 (payment) means the account approves paying the transaction's total gas fee, and bit 1 (execution) means it approves subsequent frames acting on the account's behalf as sender. Combining these yields four modes: APPROVE_NONE (0x0), APPROVE_PAYMENT (0x1), APPROVE_EXECUTION (0x2), and APPROVE_EXECUTION_AND_PAYMENT (0x3). APPROVE_SCOPE_MASK is 0x3, and the allowed scope of the executing frame is frame.flags & APPROVE_SCOPE_MASK, i.e. FRAMEPARAM(frameIndex, 0x06). An account must not approve a mode outside this allowed scope, and APPROVE_EXECUTION is valid only when the frame's resolved target is tx.sender. If verification does not succeed, the account must not call APPROVE, in which case the mode remains APPROVE_NONE and the transaction becomes invalid.

For example, when a creator makes a derivative NFT based on an original NFT, there is no standardized way to record which original the derivative references or how strong the relationship between the two tokens is. As a result, users trying to build a complex NFT ecosystem interwoven with originals and derivatives must manage relationship information their own way, which becomes harder to manage and less efficient as the ecosystem grows. As market conditions change, the value of the contract also changes, which creates counterparty credit risk: if one party defaults, the other party does not receive the payments it is owed. In addition, post-trade processing such as confirmation, valuation, settlement, and termination after execution is complex and has required reliance on central intermediaries. However, the two standards each define a Transfer(address, address, uint256) event with the same name and shape, which made it difficult for a single contract to fully comply with both standards at once. laei8da547: A diamond whose function selector mappings can be changed after deployment should implement IDiamondCut. diamondCut updates multiple functions of multiple facets in a single transaction. This is to prevent data corruption that can occur in upgrades spread over multiple transactions. For each FacetCut, if the action is Add, each entry in functionSelectors is mapped to facetAddress, and the call reverts if any selector is already mapped. If it is Replace, the mapping is changed to facetAddress, and the call reverts if the existing value equals facetAddress or the selector is empty. If it is Remove, the mapping is deleted, and the call reverts if any selector was empty. An attempt to replace or remove an immutable function must revert. Requiring the intent to be explicit in this way catches upgrade mistakes. After the function changes are done, _calldata is executed on the _init address with delegatecall to initialize or clean up data. If _init is address(0), the execution is skipped, and _calldata may then be zero bytes or arbitrary information. For interoperability, tools and UIs should expect and use this standard diamondCut function.

Because there is no size limit, gas-optimized functions for specific uses can be added, such as putting a batch transfer function in an EIP-721 implementation. Merging a structure that called several contracts in one transaction into a single diamond and accessing storage directly saves gas. A contract with few functions has cheaper call gas than one with many, so a facet can hold few external functions, and a high Solidity optimizer setting can reduce execution gas. Ways to use a function from another facet include copying the internal function code, putting a common internal function in a contract or library that several facets inherit, calling the external function in a type-safe way such as MyOtherFacet(address(this)).myFunction(arg1, arg2), looking up the facet address in selectorToFacet in storage and calling it with delegatecall, and creating an internal version of the external function and including it in the facets that need it. Two external functions with the same function signature cannot be added to one diamond at the same time. Previously, a keystore format called Web3 Secret Storage filled this role, but it had two problems. First, it uses the Keccak256 hash to compute verification values. Since BLS signatures and keys are a standard shared across multiple chains, they should not be biased toward any one chain, but Keccak is a strongly Ethereum-flavored choice and is not neutral. Second, the existing format grew by having features bolted on as needed, so it lacks structural abstraction, making it hard to swap or simplify cryptographic components. This standard defines a new keystore format for BLS12-381 keys that uses a chain-neutral hash and abstracts each cryptographic step into a module.

mdjnr2gcs6: Today each DeFi protocol reports its financial status in its own way. The criteria used to calculate assets and liabilities differ, so protocols are hard to compare, and there is no way to check status in real time, so people rely on occasional manual reports. There is also no standardized early warning when conditions worsen, so problems are sometimes noticed only after they have grown. However, the standards used to express intents keep emerging and changing. If wallets had to support each standard directly, they would need a code upgrade every time a new standard appeared, and developers of new standards would have to individually persuade wallet providers to adopt them. Without this standard, users would have to wait for their wallet to support a new intent scheme they want to use, and it would also be difficult to bundle multiple actions into one complex intent signed just once. o6xgb4b8ga: The design goal is that users can create an address first and receive funds right away, like an EOA. Account creation is handled by a factory, and initCode is interpreted as a 20-byte factory address followed by calldata. The factory is expected to use CREATE2 0xF5 rather than CREATE 0xF0 so that creation order does not affect the address, and it must return the address even if the account has already been created. A wallet obtains the pre-creation address by making a static call to entryPoint.getSenderAddress(). The EntryPoint does not call initCode directly, and the factory must verify that its createAccount() call comes from entryPoint.senderCreator(). The created address must depend on the initial signature, and a factory that accesses global storage must stake. On networks with EIP-7702 enabled, eth_sendUserOperation additionally accepts an eip7702Auth parameter, and the bundler places it in the authorizationList and executes the bundle in a SET_CODE_TX_TYPE transaction. If factory is 0x7702, the sender must be an EOA with an EIP-7702 delegation. If initCode starts with 0x7702 followed by 18 zero bytes, the first 20 bytes are replaced with the account's EIP-7702 delegation address when computing the hash, and the remainder beyond 20 bytes is used to call the account's own initialization function. This initialization function must also be callable only from entryPoint.senderCreator(). The EntryPoint cannot tell whether initialization has already happened and so may call it multiple times, so it is best to allow it only once. The EIP-7702 authorization cost PER_EMPTY_ACCOUNT_COST (25000) is not visible to the EntryPoint, so it must be included in preVerificationGas.

o8dzshps3t: Each AI agent has a unique model, memory, and character, and this data itself is the value of the agent. However, the existing NFT standard, ERC-721, was built on the assumption that metadata is fixed and visible to anyone. Agent metadata is different. To protect intellectual property it must be stored encrypted, and when ownership changes the data itself is the core of the deal, so it must be handed over in a way that keeps it secret yet verifiable. With existing standards, only token ownership changes, and there is no way to guarantee that the encrypted data was actually delivered, that the new owner can access that data, or that the agent runtime can confirm ownership and load the correct data. This standard solves the problem by bundling verification methods such as a trusted execution environment (TEE) or zero-knowledge proofs (ZKP) into a single interface.

But today these features are either built into specific account implementations or offered only through platform-specific module systems like Safe modules. As a result, users have to switch between multiple account implementations depending on which feature they want, fragmenting accounts by feature and security settings and reducing data portability. Module developers also have to choose which platform to support, leading to platform lock-in or having to build the same feature multiple times. This standard defines a common specification that coordinates the implementation work of account developers and module developers, making it possible to build modular accounts that support any module that follows the standard.

sg0mn4inmm: The address format used on Ethereum mainnet (ERC-55) is also used identically by many other blockchains. However, this format contains no information about which chain the address is intended for, so the same address can exist on multiple chains, creating ambiguity and operational risk. As a result, each protocol has created its own ad hoc method for combining addresses and chains, typically by adding a separate field or using protocol-specific conventions. This fragmentation makes cross-protocol interoperability difficult, complicates tooling, and causes notation inconsistencies at the infrastructure level. An existing text-based standard (CAIP-10) exists, but strings are inefficient to store and handle in on-chain contracts, and the chain reference length is limited to 32 characters, which cannot losslessly represent some chains. This proposal solves this problem with an extensible binary standard format that combines chain identification information and the address into one.

t49kaqs1rp: Smart contract accounts (SCAs), which operate via contract code, have become widely used since the introduction of the ERC-4337 standard, but unlike regular accounts (EOAs) that operate with a single private key, implementation code differs from wallet provider to wallet provider. As a result, they are not compatible with each other, and it is difficult for users to move an account to a different wallet service. A modular approach that assembles accounts like components has also been proposed, but its implementation cost is high and it imposes prerequisites on wallet implementations, making it unsuitable both for wallet providers who prefer their own implementation approach and for those who want to keep their contracts simple. The community currently has no general-purpose account migration standard usable with any implementation. This proposal defines a migration method that operates at the proxy (ERC-1967) layer, offering SCAs an experience similar to exporting an EOA via a private key or mnemonic.

udl2lw0kjo: A UserOperation is a structure that carries the action to be sent on behalf of a user. To avoid confusion it is not called a transaction. Like a transaction, it has nonce, callData, maxFeePerGas, maxPriorityFeePerGas, and signature. It also has sender (the account sending the action), factory and factoryData (the address and data of the factory that creates a new account, or the 0x7702 flag for an EIP-7702 account), callGasLimit (gas for the execution call), verificationGasLimit (gas for the verification step), preVerificationGas (extra gas paid to the bundler), and paymaster, paymasterVerificationGasLimit, paymasterPostOpGasLimit, and paymasterData (paymaster fields). How the signature is interpreted is decided by the account contract implementation, not by the protocol. To prevent replay across chains or across EntryPoint versions, the signature must depend on the chainid and the EntryPoint address. On-chain, a compressed PackedUserOperation is used, which bundles initCode (the factory address concatenated with factoryData, or EIP-7702 data), accountGasLimits (verificationGasLimit as 16 bytes concatenated with callGasLimit as 16 bytes), gasFees (maxPriorityFeePerGas as 16 bytes concatenated with maxFeePerGas as 16 bytes), and paymasterAndData (the paymaster fields concatenated). An EIP-7702 authorization tuple can be passed along with the UserOperation, but it is not included in the struct itself.

uh1u7z8br5: Until now, there has been no standard for presenting physical assets as NFTs with verified authenticity and ownership. Existing approaches carry at least one of two problems. First, ownership of the physical item and ownership of the NFT can drift apart. The physical item may be sold while the NFT stays put, or the NFT alone may trade while the physical item remains with someone else. Second, verifying that a physical item is genuine requires the involvement of a trusted third party such as StockX. This standard embeds a security chip that is difficult to counterfeit into the physical item and requires that chip's signature to move the NFT, offering the simplest path to binding ownership of the physical item and the digital token together without a central authority.

There is also no good way for other contracts to reliably verify the proxy's implementation address onchain, and where fixed values set at deployment (immutable arguments) are stored varies by implementation, making them hard to query. ztua58n71x: An ERC-8004 registration is itself an NFT. To have an existing NFT, such as a project, character, or collection (a master NFT), own an agent registration, the two NFTs must be linked to each other. Without this link, transferring the master NFT to someone else does not carry the ERC-8004 identity along with it; it stays with the original owner. In other words, even if a character or collection is traded, the agent's credentials or reputation record remain separate and the new owner cannot control them. This standard records, in a single standard contract per chain, which master NFT controls which agent id, so that control automatically follows when the master NFT changes hands.
